section.title: Saul Anointed King
section.sectionRationale: Samuel privately anoints Saul with oil and gives him signs to confirm God's call; the Spirit rushes on Saul and changes him. Then, publicly at Mizpah, Samuel again names Israel's demand as a rejection of God, yet casts lots, and Saul, hiding among the baggage, is chosen and proclaimed king. Some rejoice, some despise him. It is one movement: Saul is set apart as king, privately by anointing and Spirit, publicly by lot and acclamation, under the shadow of Israel's rejection of God.
section.thesis: God confirms His chosen ruler by anointing, sign, and Spirit, and openly identifies him before all Israel, yet Samuel keeps insisting that the day is one of rejection, so that Saul's coronation is joy and warning together, a king given by grace to a people who have spurned their true King.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the anointing and the promised signs, verses 1 to 8; the Spirit transforms Saul, verses 9 to 16; Saul chosen by lot at Mizpah, verses 17 to 24; and the rights of kingship and mixed response, verses 25 to 27.

units.label: The anointing and the promised signs
units.note: the LORD anointed you ruler over His inheritance

verses.text: Then Samuel took a flask of oil, poured it on Saul’s head, kissed him, and said, “Has not the LORD {{mashach|anointed}} you ruler over His inheritance?

When you leave me today, you will find two men at Rachel’s tomb in Zelzah on the border of Benjamin. They will say to you, ‘The donkeys you seek have been found, and now your father has stopped worrying about the donkeys and started worrying about you, asking, “What should I do about my son?”’

Then you will go on from there until you come to the Oak of Tabor. Three men going up to God at Bethel will meet you there, one carrying three young goats, another carrying three loaves of bread, and another carrying a skin of wine.
They will greet you and give you two loaves of bread, which you will accept from their hands.

After that you will come to Gibeah of God, where the Philistines have an outpost. As you approach the city, you will meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place, preceded by harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres, and they will be prophesying.
Then the {{ruach|Spirit of the LORD}} will rush upon you, and you will prophesy with them; and you will be transformed into a different person.
When these signs have come, do as the occasion demands, for God is with you.
And you shall go before me to Gilgal, and surely I will come to you to offer burnt offerings and to sacrifice peace offerings. Wait seven days until I come to you and show you what you are to do.”
As Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul’s heart, and all the signs came to pass that day.
When Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, a group of prophets met him. Then the Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he prophesied along with them.
When all those who had formerly known Saul saw him prophesying with the prophets, they asked one another, “What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?”
Then a man who lived there replied, “And who is their father?” So the saying became a proverb: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”
And when Saul had finished prophesying, he went up to the high place.
Now Saul’s uncle asked him and his servant, “Where did you go?” “To look for the donkeys,” Saul replied. “When we saw they were not to be found, we went to Samuel.”
“Tell me,” Saul’s uncle asked, “what did Samuel say to you?”
And Saul replied, “He assured us that the donkeys had been found.” But Saul did not tell his uncle what Samuel had said about the kingship.

units.label: Saul chosen by lot at Mizpah
units.note: Do you see the one the LORD has chosen

verses.text: After this, Samuel summoned the people to the LORD at Mizpah

and said to the Israelites, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘I brought Israel up out of Egypt, and I rescued you from the hands of the Egyptians and of all the kingdoms that oppressed you.’

But today you have rejected your God, who saves you from all your troubles and afflictions, and you have said to Him, ‘No, set a king over us.’ Now therefore present yourselves before the LORD by your tribes and clans.”
Thus Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come forward, and the tribe of Benjamin was selected.
Then he had the tribe of Benjamin come forward by its clans, and the clan of Matri was selected. Finally, Saul son of Kish was selected. But when they looked for him, they could not find him.
So again they inquired of the LORD, “Has the man come here yet?” And the LORD replied, “Behold, he has hidden himself among the baggage.”
So they ran and brought Saul, and when he stood among the people, he was a head taller than any of the others.
Samuel said to all the people, “Do you see the one the LORD has {{bachar|chosen}}? There is no one like him among all the people.” And all the people shouted, “Long live the king!”

units.label: The rights of kingship and mixed response
units.note: How can this man save us

verses.text: Then Samuel explained to the people the rights of kingship. He wrote them on a scroll and laid it up before the LORD. And Samuel sent all the people away, each to his own home.
Saul also went to his home in Gibeah, and the men of valor whose hearts God had touched went with him.
But some worthless men said, “How can this man save us?” So they despised him and brought him no gifts; but Saul remained silent about it.

mashach.gloss: To anoint, smear with oil. The pouring of oil on Saul's head sets him apart as the LORD's chosen ruler over His inheritance, God's own people. Anointing marks kings and priests as belonging to God and equipped by His Spirit; the anointed one, mashiach, ultimately points to Christ, the true and lasting Anointed King.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, wind, breath. The Spirit of the LORD rushes upon Saul, empowering him for his office and changing him into a different man. In the Old Testament the Spirit came upon judges and kings to enable God's work; here the same Spirit confirms Saul's call, though the Spirit given to Saul can later depart, unlike the abiding Spirit poured out in Christ.

bachar.gloss: To choose, select. Samuel presents Saul as the one the LORD has chosen; the king is God's choice, not merely the people's. Yet the same book will show that God's deepest choice falls on David, a man after His own heart, revealing that God chooses by the heart and directs His choosing toward the true King, Christ.

basic.context: Samuel anoints Saul in private, pouring oil on his head and naming him the LORD's chosen ruler over God's people. He gives Saul three signs to confirm the call, including that the Spirit of God will rush on him and change him into a different man, which happens that very day. Then Samuel gathers all Israel at Mizpah. He again tells them plainly that in demanding a king they have rejected the God who saves them, yet he proceeds to identify the king by lot. The lot falls on Saul, who is found hiding among the baggage. Tall and striking, he is proclaimed king with shouts of Long live the king, though some scoff, how can this man save us? The question is: how does God set apart the king Israel demanded? By His own anointing, Spirit, and choice, even while warning that the day is one of rejection.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative that holds two things together: God genuinely gives and equips Saul, and yet the whole enterprise stands under the verdict that Israel has rejected God. We should not flatten either side. The Spirit rushing on Saul is real empowering for office, not the same as saving regeneration, since this Spirit can later depart. The signs, the lot, and the anointing all show God's hand. The mixed response at the end honestly previews the reign to come. Its enduring truths are that authority comes from God and that outward gifting is not the same as a faithful heart.
basic.originalLanguages: Samuel pours oil to mashach, anoint, Saul as the LORD's chosen ruler; the word marks him as set apart to God, and its noun form is messiah. The ruach, the Spirit of the LORD, rushes on Saul to empower him and transform him for a day. And Samuel presents him as the one the LORD has bachar, chosen; the king is God's choice, though the book will show God's deepest choice resting on David and pointing to Christ.
basic.typology: Saul, anointed with oil and rushed upon by the Spirit for his office, is a shadow of the true Anointed One, on whom the Spirit rests without measure and without ever departing. The king proclaimed before all the people, yet doubted by some, how can this man save us, foreshadows Christ, God's chosen King, acclaimed by some and despised by others. And the failure that will follow Saul's gifted beginning drives the longing for the King whose heart matches His anointing.
basic.christ: Saul is anointed and Spirit-empowered, yet his gifting is not a new heart, and the Spirit given to him can be lost. Christ is the true Anointed, on whom the Spirit descended and remained, and who could not fail. Saul is presented as the LORD's chosen, but the choosing narrows through David to Jesus, God's beloved and truly chosen One. When scoffers ask, how can this man save us, they unknowingly voice the question the gospel answers: it is not Saul but Christ who can and does save. The oil on Saul's head points to the Messiah on whom it all depends.
basic.god: God is the one who appoints and equips rulers, confirming His choice by signs, Spirit, and lot, so that no one can doubt His hand. He is sovereign even over the casting of lots, directing them to His chosen man. He is honest, letting Samuel name the day's rejection even in the moment of coronation. And He touches the hearts of some to follow the king, showing that loyalty itself is His gift.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Samuel 16 records the Spirit rushing on David and later departing from Saul. Isaiah 11 promises the Spirit resting on the Messiah. Proverbs 16 says the lot's decision is from the LORD. And John 1 shows the Spirit descending and remaining on Jesus.
basic.oneStory: God sets apart Saul as king by anointing, Spirit, and lot, giving Israel the ruler they demanded even under the verdict of rejection. Yet the anointing oil, the empowering Spirit, and the language of God's chosen all reach beyond Saul to David and, at last, to Christ, the true Anointed King on whom the Spirit rests forever and who alone can save.

context.literary:
This chapter narrates Saul's anointing and public accession, continuing the account of his rise, chapters 9 to 11. It joins private confirmation, the anointing and signs, with public confirmation, the lot at Mizpah. Samuel's renewed charge of rejection, verses 18 to 19, ties back to chapter 8, and the mixed response, verse 27, sets up the vindication of Saul in chapter 11.

The three signs Samuel promises climb in intensity rather than simply repeating one another. The first confirms an ordinary fact, the donkeys are found; the second places Saul among worshipers bringing offerings up to Bethel; the third drops him into a band of ecstatic prophets and changes him into a different man. Each sign carries Saul further from the mundane errand of chapter 9 toward a properly prophetic and royal identity, so that by the time he reaches home he is, in the narrator's own words, someone else entirely.

The chapter also doubles its confirmation of Saul on purpose. Private anointing and private signs, verses 1 to 13, are matched by a public, sacred lot at Mizpah, verses 17 to 24, as though God means to leave no route of doubt open, word, sign, Spirit, and lot all pointing to the same man. And the narrator pauses a second time to explain a saying that outlived the event, is Saul also among the prophets, verse 12, exactly as an earlier aside explained the old word for prophet in chapter 9. Both asides tell the reader that this story was being handed down, remembered, and still being talked about long after Samuel and Saul themselves were gone.
context.historical:
Anointing with oil formally installed kings in Israel and the ancient Near East. Prophetic bands, accompanied by music and ecstatic prophecy, were known in this period. Casting lots was a recognized means of seeking God's decision. The rights of kingship written on a scroll and stored before the LORD reflect the law's provision that the king be bound under God's word, Deuteronomy 17. Gibeah was Saul's hometown.

Bethel, where the second sign sends Saul, was already an ancient and revered worship site by Samuel's day, the very place Jacob had once named the house of God after his vision of a stairway to heaven, Genesis 28:16-19, so the men Saul meets there are not casual travelers but pilgrims bringing goats, bread, and wine up to a place already thick with covenant history. Companies of prophets moving with harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres reflect a known feature of this period, groups given to shared, music-accompanied prophesying, distinct from the settled office a single seer like Samuel held.

Samuel's act of writing the rights of kingship on a scroll and laying it before the LORD, verse 25, follows a recognized pattern of depositing a binding document in a sanctuary, the way Joshua once recorded Israel's covenant renewal in the Book of the Law of God and set up a witness stone at the sanctuary, Joshua 24:26-27, and the way Moses commanded that the Book of the Law be kept beside the ark itself as a witness, Deuteronomy 31:24-26. Saul's kingship, from its very first day, is filed as a subordinate document next to God's own law, not as a replacement for it.
context.canonical:
The anointing and Spirit-empowerment of the king develop the messianic thread from Hannah's song and the oracle to Eli. The pattern of the Spirit coming upon a king, and the later warning that He can depart from Saul, prepares for the promise of a Spirit-anointed Messiah in Isaiah and its fulfillment in Jesus, on whom the Spirit remains.

The Spirit rushing upon Saul repeats a formula the book of Judges used again and again, on Othniel, Judges 3:10, on Gideon, Judges 6:34, on Jephthah, Judges 11:29, and on Samson, Judges 14:6, each time raising up someone to act for God's people in a moment of crisis. Placing Saul in that same line tells the canon's story of leadership as continuous, judges and then a king given the same enabling Spirit, though only the king's line will eventually receive the promise of an anointed one on whom the Spirit rests without measure or interruption, Isaiah 11:1-2 and Isaiah 61:1.

The scorn some voice at Saul's coronation, how can this man save us, verse 27, anticipates a pattern that recurs whenever God's chosen deliverer first appears unimpressive to the people meant to receive him. Centuries later Nathanael will ask of another surprising candidate from an unlikely place, can anything good come out of Nazareth, John 1:46, before becoming one of the twelve. Scripture is honest that God's anointed ones are regularly doubted at their first appearing, and that the doubt itself becomes part of the record rather than something the narrator hides.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
To show that Saul is genuinely set apart as king by God's anointing, Spirit, and choice, while keeping before the reader that the day of coronation is also a day of Israel's rejection of God, and to introduce the tension between outward gifting and a faithful heart.

The author wants a reader who has just heard, in chapter 8, that asking for a king was itself a rejection of the LORD to see that God's generosity did not require Him to pretend the request was harmless. He piles up confirmation after confirmation of Saul, a private anointing, three fulfilled signs, a transformed heart, a public lot, and a shout of acclamation, precisely so that no one could later claim Saul lacked legitimate standing. Yet in the very same speech Samuel will not let the word rejected go unsaid, verses 18 and 19, because the writer intends both truths to be held at once, God's gift is real, and Israel's sin in demanding it is also real.

The author is also laying groundwork for what is coming. By showing that being seized by the Spirit and changed into a different man did not, by itself, guarantee a faithful king, the narrative quietly warns the reader not to equate visible religious experience with a settled, obedient heart, a distinction the book will press hard once Saul's later disobedience is exposed in chapters 13 and 15.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes Saul's anointing and the Spirit rushing upon him; it does not prescribe seeking ecstatic experiences or casting lots for guidance today. What endures is that authority is given by God, that His Spirit equips for service, and that spiritual gifting must not be mistaken for a transformed, faithful heart.

Nobody reading this chapter is meant to go looking for prophetic bands with harps and tambourines as proof of a call, or to cast lots before making decisions; those were the recognized means of guidance for Israel in that specific covenant moment, not standing instructions for every era. What the chapter does hand forward is a caution worth keeping: a real, even dramatic, encounter with God's Spirit changed Saul for a day, and the people rightly asked, is Saul also among the prophets, yet that same man will later disobey God outright. Being used, moved, or gifted by God is not the same as being faithful to Him over years, and readers are meant to examine their own hearts rather than rest on any past experience as proof of present standing.

debates.question: What does it mean that the Spirit rushed on Saul and he was changed into a different man?

views.label: Empowerment for office, not saving regeneration
views.case: The Spirit came upon judges and kings to equip them for a task; Saul is enabled and outwardly transformed for kingship, but this is not the same as a new heart, since the same Spirit later departs from him, 1 Samuel 16:14.

views.label: A genuine, if temporary, work confirming his call
views.case: God really changed Saul's heart, verse 9, and the Spirit's coming authenticated him before the people; the change was real and God-given, even though it did not guarantee lifelong faithfulness.

debates.bearing: Both agree that spiritual empowerment is not the same as persevering faith; Saul's gifting warns that being used by God is no substitute for a heart that follows Him, and points to the abiding Spirit given in Christ.

debates.question: Why does Samuel proclaim the king yet also declare the day a rejection of God?

views.label: To hold grace and warning together
views.case: God graciously gives and equips the king the people demanded, yet Samuel refuses to let them forget that the request rejected God's own kingship; the coronation is mercy and rebuke at once.

views.label: To bind the monarchy under God from the start
views.case: By naming the rejection and writing the rights of kingship before the LORD, Samuel sets the king under God's word and verdict, so the monarchy begins accountable to God rather than autonomous.

debates.bearing: Either way the chapter teaches that God's gifts do not cancel His truth; the king and the people stand under God's word, and true kingship must submit to the LORD, fulfilled in Christ.

study.originalLanguages:
Samuel's anointing is sealed with an unusual and pointed gesture, he kissed him, verse 1, using the same Hebrew verb, nashaq, that later names the homage owed to God's anointed king, Kiss the Son, lest He be angry, Psalm 2:12. A prophet who has just told Israel that their request is a rejection of the LORD nonetheless bends to honor the man that same LORD has chosen, a small but real picture of proper submission to a ruler God Himself installs.

Mashach, to anoint, and ruach, the Spirit that rushes on Saul, together mark him as God's man for the office, set apart by oil and by power at once. The description of Saul's transformation, turned into a different man, describes a genuine, observable change of behavior, strong enough that people who had always known him ask what has happened to the son of Kish, yet the same book will later use identical language, the Spirit rushed upon him, for both David's empowering, 1 Samuel 16:13, and, chillingly, for an evil spirit that torments Saul once God's Spirit has departed, 1 Samuel 16:14 and 18:10. The vocabulary of empowering does not by itself guarantee which spirit is doing the empowering.

The lot narrows Saul out of all Israel step by step, tribe, then clan, then man, and the BSB uses the same word, selected, for each stage of that process, exactly as it uses selected for the stepwise process that narrows the guilty Achan out of all Israel, tribe, then clan, then family, then man, Joshua 7:16-18. One process finally catches a hidden sinner, the other finally catches a hidden king, and the same careful, public, step by step exposure lies behind both, a reminder that the LORD who can expose sin this way can just as surely appoint a ruler this way.

And Samuel presents the man the lot has caught as the one the LORD has bachar, chosen, a verb that will recur soon enough for God's deeper choice of David, 1 Samuel 16:8-10, and that ultimately gathers itself into the New Testament's own title for Jesus at the transfiguration, This is My Son, whom I have chosen, Luke 9:35, the beloved Son in whom the Father is well pleased and to whom every earlier choosing was only ever pointing.

typology.type: The king anointed with oil and rushed upon by the Spirit
typology.fulfillment: Oil and Spirit together mark Saul for office, yet in his case the two do not guarantee each other, since a chapter later this very Spirit will depart from him, 1 Samuel 16:14. John the Baptist later testifies that he saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove and resting on Jesus, a remaining the Baptist stresses precisely because it was not the ordinary pattern, John 1:32-33. Saul's anointing is a moment; Christ's is a permanent possession, the very difference the whole Old Testament pattern was quietly building toward.

typology.type: The chosen king acclaimed by some and despised by others
typology.fulfillment: Most of Israel shouts long live the king, while some worthless men ask how can this man save us and refuse him any gift, verse 27. Peter later describes Jesus in nearly the same terms, a living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight, precious to those who believe, but to those who do not believe, a stone of stumbling, 1 Peter 2:4-8. Saul's mixed reception is the first small instance of a pattern that meets God's Anointed at every stage.

typology.type: The gifted king whose heart will not match his calling
typology.fulfillment: Saul receives a genuinely new heart for a day, verse 9, and yet the years ahead will show that a moment's transformation is not the same as an abiding one. The writer to the Hebrews says of the Son, You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness, therefore God, Your God, has anointed You, a King whose character and calling are never out of step with each other, Hebrews 1:8-9. Saul's gifting outruns his obedience; Christ's obedience never falls short of His anointing.

study.christ:
Samuel kisses the man he has just anointed, an unusual gesture that the Psalms will later turn into an instruction for the whole world, Kiss the Son, lest He be angry, and blessed are all who take refuge in Him, Psalm 2:12. What is a private moment of homage to Saul becomes, in Christ, the standing posture every person owes to God's true Anointed King.

The private confirmations Saul receives, that the donkeys are found, that worshipers will greet him at Bethel, that prophets will meet him with music, are all fulfilled that very day, verse 9, proof that God keeps small promises as carefully as large ones. Yet none of them changes Saul permanently. The Spirit that rushes on him will one day rush on David instead and depart from Saul entirely, 1 Samuel 16:13-14, a possibility the text never even raises for Jesus, on whom John saw the Spirit descending and resting, John 1:32-33, without interruption or reversal, because the Father gives the Spirit without limit to the One He has sent, John 3:34.

Saul is presented at Mizpah as the one the LORD has chosen, and the crowd's response splits at once, some hailing him, long live the king, others sneering, how can this man save us. That same split will follow God's true Chosen One, whom the Father names at the transfiguration in almost identical words, This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him, Luke 9:35, and whom Peter will describe as a stone precious to believers yet a stumbling block to others, 1 Peter 2:4-8. Being God's anointed has never guaranteed universal acclaim, in Saul's day or in Christ's.

And Samuel's careful act of writing the rights of kingship and laying them before the LORD, verse 25, quietly anticipates a King who does not merely receive a law to keep but is Himself the reality every scroll in Israel's law and prophets was written to describe, Luke 24:44. Saul is handed a scroll to obey; Christ fulfills what the scroll could only foreshadow.
study.god:
God confirms Saul by every means available to Him at once, word, sign, oil, Spirit, lot, and crowd, as though refusing to leave His choice open to any honest doubt. Three separate and unrelated signs, involving strangers Saul has never met, all come true within a single day, verse 9, which is the kind of precision that belongs only to the God who sees the whole of a day before it happens.

He is a God who can be trusted with the smallest mechanisms of communal life. When Israel narrows a king out of twelve tribes by a sacred lot, tribe, then clan, then man, the text never suggests that chance is loose in the process; the same procedure that catches a hidden sinner elsewhere in Israel's story, Joshua 7:16-18, catches a hidden king here. Whether the lot is exposing guilt or appointing a ruler, the same divine hand is behind it.

He is honest even while being generous. Samuel does not soften the charge of rejection to make the coronation feel better, verses 18 and 19; God allows His prophet to name Israel's sin plainly on the very day He is granting Israel's request, because His gifts have never depended on pretending His people are faultless. Grace, in this chapter, does not require amnesia.

He is also a God who gives and can withdraw His enabling presence without ceasing to be just. The Spirit that rushes on Saul and changes him into a different man is a real gift, not a trick, yet the same book will later record that Spirit departing, 1 Samuel 16:14, a sober reminder that God's empowering is never something a person owns outright. What He grants, He remains free to reclaim, and what looks like present favor is never a guarantee of unconditional future standing.

Finally He is a God who moves hearts rather than merely commanding outward compliance. Verse 26 says plainly that the men who followed Saul home were men whose hearts God had touched, which means even loyalty to God's appointed king is, at bottom, something God supplies rather than something people simply decide to do on their own.

crossReferences.note: The same verb rushed describes the Spirit coming on Saul here and coming on David a few chapters later, but this time paired with the report that the Spirit had departed from Saul entirely. Being empowered once is shown to be no guarantee of being empowered permanently.

The Spirit of the LORD will rest on the coming branch from Jesse's line, described with an abundance, wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, the very opposite of a Spirit that can be given and later withdrawn. Saul's temporary anointing only sharpens the wonder of a King whose Spirit never lifts.

The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision belongs to the LORD. Israel narrows its king out from twelve tribes to one man by a sacred lot, and the proverb states plainly what the narrative shows at length, that the outcome was never left to chance.

Christ is described as a living stone, rejected by men yet chosen and precious in God's sight, precious to those who believe but a stone of stumbling to those who do not. Saul's coronation splits Israel the same way, some shouting long live the king, others despising him outright.

Kiss the Son, lest He be angry. The homage the psalm demands for God's true King is pictured in miniature by the same gesture, a kiss, that Samuel privately gives Saul at his anointing, verse 1, a small enacted picture of what the whole world owes the greater Anointed One.

Israel is narrowed by lot, tribe, clan, family, then man, to expose Achan's hidden sin, and the BSB uses the very word selected for each stage, the identical word it uses when Israel is narrowed the same way to reveal Saul. One process exposes guilt, the other reveals God's chosen ruler.

At the transfiguration the Father names Jesus in words that echo Samuel's charge over Saul, This is My Son, whom I have chosen. Listen to Him. What Samuel could only announce of a flawed man chosen for a season, the Father declares directly and finally of His own Son.

God gives the Spirit without limit to the One He has sent, a phrase that stands in deliberate contrast to Saul, whose portion of the Spirit was real but limited enough in time that it could later be withdrawn, 1 Samuel 16:14.

Joshua likewise records Israel's covenant renewal and sets up a witness stone at the sanctuary, the same pattern Samuel follows when he writes the rights of kingship on a scroll and lays it up before the LORD, binding the new king under the same God who bound the nation at Shechem.

study.oneStory:
By the time Saul is anointed, Israel already has centuries of pattern behind it, God raises up a deliverer, His Spirit rushes on that person, the people are saved, and then, given enough time, everyone forgets and needs saving again. Judges after judge follows that circuit. This chapter folds a king into the very same rhythm, the identical Spirit, the identical rushing, so that Israel's first king begins his reign standing exactly where its judges once stood, dependent on a gift he did not generate and cannot keep by his own effort.

The difference a king introduces is permanence, or at least the hope of it, a throne rather than a rotating cast of deliverers. Yet this chapter refuses to let that hope rest on Saul himself. Even at the height of confirmation, oil, sign, Spirit, lot, and shouting crowd, Samuel will not stop saying the word rejected, because the deeper problem, a people who would rather see a king than trust an invisible LORD, has not actually been solved by giving them one.

The generations after Saul will keep discovering this. David is chosen next, closer to what God wanted but still flawed and mortal. Every king after him in Israel and Judah will eventually disappoint in the same basic way, gifted for a while, faithful for a while, and then not. The chapter's own vocabulary, anointed, chosen, Spirit, quietly keeps the reader's hope moving past every one of them, until it settles on a Son whom the Father names Chosen without qualification, on whom the Spirit rests without measure and without end, and whose kingdom, unlike Saul's fragile one, cannot be swept away. What Israel receives at Mizpah in a mixture of joy and doubt, the world receives at last in Christ without either flaw or expiration.

quiz.q: How did Samuel first set Saul apart as king?

options.text: He privately anointed Saul with oil as the LORD's chosen ruler and gave him confirming signs.
options.note: Verses 1 to 8; the anointing and signs mark Saul as God's chosen before the public event.

options.text: He poured oil on Saul's head and called him ruler over God's inheritance.
options.note: True, but omits the confirming signs, including the Spirit, that accompanied the anointing.

options.text: He crowned Saul publicly before all Israel first.
options.note: The public choosing came later at Mizpah; the anointing was first and private.

options.text: He had the people vote for Saul as king.
options.note: Saul was chosen by God through anointing and lot, not by a vote.

quiz.q: What happened when the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon Saul?

options.text: He prophesied and was transformed into a different man, empowered for his office.
options.note: Verses 6 and 9 to 10; the Spirit equipped and changed Saul for kingship.

options.text: He prophesied along with the group of prophets.
options.note: True, but omits the deeper point that he was transformed and empowered for his calling.

options.text: He was permanently made righteous and could never fail.
options.note: The empowering was real but not a guarantee of faithfulness; the Spirit later departs from Saul.

options.text: Nothing visible happened to him at all.
options.note: The change was evident enough that people asked, is Saul also among the prophets?

quiz.q: What did Samuel declare even as Saul was made king at Mizpah?

options.text: That in demanding a king the people had rejected the God who saves them.
options.note: Verses 18 to 19 name the day's rejection even amid the coronation.

options.text: That God had brought Israel up out of Egypt and rescued them.
options.note: True, and Samuel said it, but the pointed word was that they had now rejected that God.

options.text: That the people had done well to ask for a king.
options.note: The opposite; Samuel called it a rejection of God.

options.text: That Saul would be a perfect and faithful king.
options.note: Samuel gave no such assurance; he warned of rejection and wrote the rights of kingship.

quiz.q: How did the people respond to Saul as king?

options.text: Many shouted Long live the king and followed him, but some scoffers said, how can this man save us?
options.note: Verses 24 to 27 show a divided response, joy and contempt together.

options.text: The whole nation joyfully accepted him without exception.
options.note: Most acclaimed him, but the text notes worthless men who despised him.

options.text: Everyone rejected Saul and refused to follow him.
options.note: The opposite; men of valor followed him and the people shouted Long live the king.

options.text: They immediately removed him from the throne.
options.note: Saul was proclaimed king, not removed.

quiz.q: How does Saul's anointing and empowering point forward to Christ?

options.text: The oil and the Spirit point to Christ, the true Anointed on whom the Spirit remains and who alone can save.
options.note: Saul's temporary anointing foreshadows the Messiah's abiding one, John 1:32-33.

options.text: It shows that God equips leaders with His Spirit for their work.
options.note: True, but stops short of Christ, the true Anointed the oil and Spirit foreshadow.

options.text: It teaches that anyone filled with the Spirit becomes sinless.
options.note: Saul's later failure shows empowering is not the same as a perfected heart.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The anointing and Spirit clearly point to the Messiah, Jesus.

questions: The Spirit changed Saul, yet his heart later turned away. How does his story warn you that being gifted or used by God is not the same as walking faithfully with Him?
Saul was proclaimed king even as Samuel called the day a rejection of God. Where might God be graciously giving you what you asked for, while calling you to examine your heart?
Some followed Saul because God touched their hearts, while others despised him. What softens or hardens a heart toward God's appointed King, Jesus?
Saul hid among the baggage on the day of his calling. When has fear or reluctance made you hide from what God was calling you to, and how did God draw you out?
The scoffers asked, how can this man save us? How does the gospel answer that question, not in Saul but in Christ, the King who truly saves?

translationNotes.note: The Hebrew is brief; the BSB footnote records a longer Septuagint reading that expands the anointing charge, but the main text follows the Hebrew, anointed you ruler over His inheritance.
Gibeah of God renders the Hebrew Gibeath-Elohim, the hill of God; the place names playing on the hill recur through the chapter.
They inquired of the LORD, likely by lot or oracle, and were told Saul had hidden among the baggage, underscoring both God's knowledge and Saul's reluctance.

A Dead Sea Scrolls manuscript adds a paragraph here about Nahash the Ammonite oppressing Gad and Reuben, giving background to the siege of Jabesh-gilead in chapter 11; the BSB follows the Masoretic Text and Septuagint, which omit it.
